title: Tired, thirsty and up at night: fatigue in a 33-year-old mechanic
desc: This station involves a focused history and examination of a 33-year-old mechanic with 5 months of fatigue, thirst and nocturia. The candidate then interprets his urine dipstick, fasting bloods and urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio, makes a new diagnosis of type 2 diabetes, and plans initial management and safety netting in general practice.
focus: Fatigue in a young adult: a broad screening history that finds the osmotic symptoms, then diagnosing and starting management of type 2 diabetes in general practice
stem: You are a final-year medical student on placement in a suburban general practice. Skye, a 33-year-old mechanic, has come to see you because he has been tired and low on energy for the past 5 months. Your GP supervisor will see him after you.
tasks: Take a focused history from Skye and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining and why (10 minutes).
The examiner will give you Skye's urine dipstick, fasting blood results and urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio. Interpret them, then outline your management approach and safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Skye, a 33-year-old mechanic. You are easy-going but fed up with feeling flat. You are a bit defensive about your weight and diet if the candidate sounds judgemental. The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings below when the candidate says what they would examine.

Opening line: "I've just been so tired for months, doc. No energy at all. I don't know what's going on."

The tiredness (give only when asked):

  • It has crept up over the last 5 months or so. No trigger: no recent illness, no flu, no new stress at work or home.
  • You need more sleep than before, but extra sleep does not help. You still wake up tired.
  • You used to go to the gym 3 times a week. You have stopped because you have no energy.
  • You are still getting through work, but you drag yourself home and crash on the couch.

Urine and thirst (give only when asked about sleep, the toilet or drinking):

  • You get up to pass urine 3 or 4 times a night. This is what worries you most: it wrecks your sleep. You have stopped drinking anything after dinner and it has made no difference.
  • You pass a lot of urine during the day too.
  • You are thirsty all the time. You drink well over 3 litres of water a day, plus a couple of cans of soft drink at work.
  • No pain or burning passing urine, no blood, no trouble starting or a weak stream.

Weight: you have put on about 20 kg over the last few years. You have not lost any weight recently.

Other symptoms (all no, if asked):

  • No blurred vision, no tingling or numbness in the feet or hands. No boils, thrush or slow-healing cuts.
  • No feeling cold, constipation, dry skin or hair change.
  • No breathlessness, palpitations, blood in the bowel motions or black motions. No change in bowel habit.
  • No fevers, night sweats, lumps or bruising.
  • No bone pain, kidney stones, tummy pain or confusion.
  • No ankle swelling, itch, chest pain, cough, coughing blood or yellow skin.
  • Never had a head injury or brain surgery. Never taken lithium.
  • If asked about snoring, sleepiness or driving: "My partner says I snore a bit, but she hasn't noticed me stop breathing." You do not fall asleep at the wheel or feel drowsy driving.

Mood (if asked): "A bit fed up with being tired, but I'm not depressed." You still enjoy your kids, footy and mates. No thoughts of harming yourself or of suicide.

Past medical history: high cholesterol for 5 years, high blood pressure for 2 years. No operations or hospital admissions.

Medicines: atorvastatin and perindopril (you do not remember the doses). You take them most days. No over-the-counter medicines or supplements. No allergies.

Family history: your mum died a couple of years ago of a heart attack at 66. She had type 2 diabetes for years. Your dad died of bowel (colon) cancer at 79. Your son (8) and daughter (5) are healthy.

Social history:

  • Mechanic at a local workshop. You live with your partner and two kids.
  • Smoking: about a pack a week, since you were 13 (20 years).
  • Alcohol: 1 or 2 glasses of wine every night.
  • No recreational drugs.
  • Diet: lots of takeaway (fish and chips), soft drinks and microwave dinners. "I don't really cook."

Ideas, concerns, expectations:

  • Idea: you are probably just working too hard and getting older.
  • Concern: getting up to pass urine several times a night and never sleeping properly.
  • Expectation: some blood tests and something to help you sleep through the night.

Question to raise once the urinary symptoms have been asked about: "Why do I keep needing to wee at night, even when I stop drinking before bed?"

Exam findings (examiner: give only when the candidate says what they examine):

  • General: alert, comfortable, central obesity. Neck circumference 43 cm. Well hydrated, mucous membranes moist. No pallor or jaundice. Affect reactive.
  • Observations: BP 142/88 mmHg (repeat 140/86). HR 84/min, regular. RR 14/min. SpO2 98% on room air. Temperature 36.6 °C. Weight 112 kg, height 178 cm, BMI 35.3 kg/m², waist 118 cm.
  • Capillary blood glucose (if asked): 14.6 mmol/L, random (about 2 hours after lunch).
  • Urine dipstick (if asked): "The practice nurse is testing it; the result will be given to you in Part 2."
  • Skin: velvety darkened skin at the back of the neck and in both axillae (acanthosis nigricans). Several skin tags on the neck. No boils, fungal infection or xanthelasma.
  • Neck: no goitre or thyroid nodule. No cervical, supraclavicular or axillary lymphadenopathy.
  • Cardiovascular and respiratory: heart sounds dual, no murmur. JVP not raised. No ankle oedema. Chest clear.
  • Abdomen: obese, soft, non-tender. Liver and spleen not palpable (limited by habitus). No masses. No stigmata of chronic liver disease.
  • Eyes: visual acuity 6/6 in each eye. Undilated fundoscopy: limited view, no obvious abnormality.
  • Feet: skin intact, no callus or ulcers. Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses palpable. 10 g monofilament felt at all sites; vibration normal at the great toes.
  • Neurological: ankle reflexes present with a normal relaxation phase.

check.x: Professionalism
Hand hygiene, introduces self and role, confirms Skye's identity, explains the purpose of the consultation, and gains consent for the examination.
Starts with open questions, is non-judgemental about his weight, diet, smoking and alcohol, uses plain language, and acknowledges how much the night-time toilet trips bother him.
History
Characterises the fatigue:

kids.x: Onset and course: gradual over about 5 months, with no trigger, recent illness or new stressor.
Impact and sleep: needs more sleep but extra sleep does not help; has stopped exercising (was going 3 times a week).

check.x: Asks about osmotic symptoms and weight:

kids.x: Nocturia 3 or 4 times a night despite drinking less before bed, and daytime polyuria.
Thirst: over 3 L of water a day plus soft drinks.
Weight change: about 20 kg gained over the last few years, no recent loss.

check.x: Asks about features of complications or infection: blurred vision, tingling or numbness in the feet, recurrent skin, genital or urinary infections [none].
Screens for other causes of fatigue and polyuria with symptom clusters:
check.d: Tick each cluster asked about. Five or more of seven clusters = full marks; 3 to 4 = partial; fewer than 3 = not awarded.

kids.x: Hypothyroidism: cold intolerance, constipation, dry skin or hair change [none].
Anaemia or iron deficiency: breathlessness, palpitations, rectal bleeding or melaena [none].
Diabetes insipidus: lithium, head injury or brain surgery [none].
Hypercalcaemia: bone pain, kidney stones, abdominal pain, constipation or confusion [none].
Malignancy, including haematological: fevers, night sweats, weight loss, lumps, bruising or change in bowel habit [none].
Chronic kidney, heart, lung or liver disease: swelling, itch, chest pain, breathlessness, cough or haemoptysis, jaundice [none].
Sleep: snoring, witnessed apnoeas, daytime sleepiness or drowsy driving [snores a bit, no apnoeas, no drowsy driving].

check.x: Screens for depression and substance use, including low mood, anhedonia, recreational drugs and suicidal ideation [mood fine, still enjoys things, no drugs, no suicidal thoughts].
check.d: Critical core = asks about mood or anhedonia AND suicidal ideation; recreational drug use is credit.

check.x: Takes the past medical history: high cholesterol for 5 years, hypertension for 2 years, no surgery or admissions.
Takes a medication history with adherence and allergies: atorvastatin and perindopril, taken most days; no allergies.
Takes the family history: mother had type 2 diabetes and died of a heart attack at 66, father died of colon cancer at 79, son and daughter healthy.
Takes a social history:

kids.x: Smoking quantified: about a pack a week for 20 years.
Alcohol quantified: 1 or 2 glasses of wine every night.
Diet and activity: takeaway, soft drinks and microwave dinners; no exercise now.
Occupation and home: mechanic, lives with his partner and two children.

check.x: Explores his ideas, concerns and expectations: thinks he is overworked and getting older, is most worried about the nocturia ruining his sleep, and expects blood tests and help to sleep through.
Examination
General inspection and vital signs, with weight, height, BMI and waist circumference [BP 142/88, HR 84, BMI 35.3, waist 118 cm].
Requests a capillary blood glucose [14.6 mmol/L random].
check.d: Credit, but do not require: also asks for a urine dipstick (the result is given in Part 2).

check.x: Looks for signs of insulin resistance and assesses hydration [acanthosis nigricans at the neck and axillae, skin tags; well hydrated].
Looks for baseline complications: visual acuity and fundoscopy, and the feet (skin, pulses, monofilament or vibration) [all normal].
Examines for other causes of fatigue: thyroid and reflexes, conjunctival pallor, lymph nodes, abdomen for liver or masses, JVP and ankle oedema, chest [all normal].
check.d: Award for any four of these.

check.x: Interpretation

Urine dipstick: glucose 3+ (heavy glycosuria) with ketones negative and specific gravity 1.020. Explains that glycosuria causes an osmotic diuresis that explains his polyuria, nocturia and thirst; that urine which is not dilute (DI typically gives SG 1.005 or less) and is full of glucose is against diabetes insipidus; and that no ketones is against ketoacidosis.
HbA1c 9.1% (76 mmol/mol) and fasting glucose 12.4 mmol/L are diagnostic of diabetes; no repeat test is needed (symptomatic, and two different tests are abnormal).
States that the normal FBC, iron studies, TSH, corrected calcium and renal function are against anaemia, iron deficiency, hypothyroidism, hypercalcaemia and CKD as causes of his fatigue.

Interprets the incidental results: raised ALT/GGT as probable MASLD and/or alcohol; high TG and low HDL as the insulin-resistance pattern with LDL 3.0 above goal on atorvastatin; normal uACR and eGFR as baseline, so metformin is safe (award for two of three).
check.d: LDL goal: RACGP handbook lipid target in type 2 diabetes is LDL below 2.0 mmol/L.

check.x: Gives new type 2 diabetes as the most likely diagnosis, with obesity and metabolic syndrome (central obesity, hypertension, dyslipidaemia), justified by the symptoms, weight gain, family history, diet, acanthosis and results.
Names differentials, each with a feature for or against from this case: diabetes insipidus, hypothyroidism, depression, and type 1 diabetes or LADA (obese, no weight loss, no ketones).
check.d: Award for at least three with a reason each. Credit malignancy (normal FBC and calcium, no weight loss). Credit OSA (snoring, obesity, hypertension; no witnessed apnoeas).

check.x: Management
Explains the diagnosis in plain language, linking the high sugar to his tiredness, thirst and night-time urination, and checks his understanding.
Gives lifestyle advice:

kids.x: Smoking cessation with support (Quitline 13 78 48, nicotine replacement or varenicline).
Alcohol: no more than 10 standard drinks a week and no more than 4 on any day.
At least 150 minutes of moderate activity a week (plus resistance exercise), aiming for 5 to 10% weight loss.
Diet: swap soft drinks for water, cut down takeaway, see a dietitian.

check.x: Starts metformin as first-line therapy, at a low dose with meals and increased slowly, warning about gut side effects.
check.d: Credit: plans an add-on agent (SGLT2 inhibitor, GLP-1 receptor agonist, DPP-4 inhibitor or sulfonylurea) if HbA1c is still above target at 3 months, with insulin later if needed. Example (eTG): metformin 500 mg once daily with the evening meal, increased every 1 to 2 weeks to 1 g twice daily as tolerated (or modified-release 500 mg once daily up to 2 g once daily). Credit: an individualised HbA1c target, generally 7.0% (53 mmol/mol) or less. Credit: considers early combination therapy (e.g. adding an SGLT2 inhibitor or GLP-1 receptor agonist) because HbA1c is more than 1.5% above target, or a GLP-1 RA for weight, subject to PBS criteria.

check.x: Sets up team care: a GP chronic condition management plan with a diabetes educator, dietitian and exercise physiologist, and NDSS registration.

Plans baseline complication screening and cardiovascular risk management: retinal examination now, yearly uACR and eGFR, and addresses his BP above target: aim below 130/80 for people with diabetes, if tolerated (Australian guideline for assessing and managing cardiovascular disease risk 2023; RACGP handbook). Both readings (142/88 and 140/86) are above this. Confirms with home or ambulatory readings, then up-titrates perindopril.
check.d: Critical core = arranges retinal screening AND acts on the BP; the yearly uACR/eGFR is credit. Credit: a yearly foot check, and reviewing statin adherence and dose (LDL 3.0). Credit: yearly influenza and pneumococcal vaccination; no routine home glucose testing on metformin alone.

check.x: Safety netting

Says vomiting, abdominal pain, fast or deep breathing, drowsiness or confusion, or being unable to keep fluids down need ED (000 if very unwell). Advises withholding metformin while vomiting or dehydrated.
check.d: Credit: if an SGLT2 inhibitor is started, withhold it during acute illness, poor intake or before surgery, because of the risk of euglycaemic ketoacidosis. Credit: also withhold perindopril while vomiting or dehydrated (sick-day rules).

check.x: Says to see the GP sooner for worsening thirst or urination, unexpected weight loss, blurred vision, infections, or metformin side effects he cannot tolerate.
Arranges follow-up: review in 2 to 4 weeks (metformin tolerance, BP, the plan) and HbA1c in 3 months.
check.d: Credit: the yearly cycle of care, and written information (Diabetes Australia, NDSS).

part2.lead: Here is the urine dipstick the practice nurse did at Skye's visit, and the fasting blood and urine results from two days later. Skye has come back to discuss them.
part2.patient:
Skye is in the room for Part 2. He says nothing during the handover. While the candidate explains the plan (Questions 3 and 4), put these questions:

  • When metformin comes up: "So am I going to end up on insulin needles?"
  • When alcohol or smoking come up: "Do I have to give up the wine completely?"

Be relieved that there is an explanation for the night-time toilet trips.

handover.label: Urine dipstick (practice nurse, first visit)
handover.result: Mid-stream urine, tested with a dipstick in the treatment room during the first visit.
handover.model:
• Read: glucose 3+ (heavy glycosuria), ketones negative, specific gravity 1.020, not dilute. Protein, blood, leucocytes and nitrites are negative.
  • For Skye: heavy glycosuria means his blood glucose is above the renal threshold (about 10 mmol/L), so glucose drags water into the urine. This osmotic diuresis explains his polyuria, his nocturia that does not settle when he drinks less, and his thirst. In diabetes insipidus the urine is dilute (SG typically 1.005 or less) and has no glucose, so urine that is not dilute and is full of glucose argues strongly against it. No ketones means no ketoacidosis and no marked insulin deficiency. There is no sign of a urinary infection.
  • What it changes: it points to diabetes, to be confirmed with a laboratory glucose and HbA1c. He does not need urgent hospital transfer.

handover.label: Fasting bloods
handover.result: Fasting sample collected at 08:05. Lab comment: HbA1c of 6.5% (48 mmol/mol) or more is consistent with diabetes mellitus.
handover.model:
• Read: HbA1c 9.1% (76 mmol/mol) and fasting glucose 12.4 mmol/L, both well above the diagnostic thresholds (6.5% or 48 mmol/mol; 7.0 mmol/L). FBC, ferritin and transferrin saturation are normal. Sodium, potassium, creatinine and eGFR are normal. Corrected calcium and TSH are normal. ALT 64 and GGT 92 are mildly raised, with normal bilirubin, ALP and albumin. On atorvastatin, triglycerides are 3.4 (high), HDL 0.8 (low) and LDL 3.0.
  • For Skye: diabetes is confirmed: he is symptomatic and two different tests are abnormal, so no repeat is needed. The normal results argue against anaemia, iron deficiency, hypothyroidism, hypercalcaemia and CKD as causes of his fatigue. The liver enzymes suggest fatty liver (MASLD) and/or alcohol. High triglycerides with low HDL is the typical lipid pattern of insulin resistance.
  • What it changes: start lifestyle change and metformin. RACGP handbook lipid target in type 2 diabetes: LDL below 2.0 mmol/L; LDL 3.0 is above this, so confirm daily adherence, then increase the atorvastatin dose (or add ezetimibe). Recheck LFTs once he drinks less and loses weight. Check hepatitis B and C serology (iron studies already normal) as part of excluding other causes. Consider liver ultrasound and, as he gets older, fibrosis assessment (FIB-4 is not validated under 35; elastography if concerned).

labs.title: Full blood count and iron studies
Electrolytes, renal, bone and liver function

rows.n: Diagnostic of diabetes at 6.5% or more
Diagnostic of diabetes at 48 or more

handover.label: Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio
handover.result: Early morning (first void) urine, collected with the fasting bloods.
handover.model:
• Read: uACR 0.6 mg/mmol, well below the male reference of under 2.5, with an eGFR over 90.
  • For Skye: no albuminuria or reduced kidney function at diagnosis. This is his baseline.
  • What it changes: metformin can be started with no dose adjustment. Repeat uACR and eGFR at least yearly as part of the annual cycle of care.

ask: You are now handing over to your GP supervisor. Please give an ISBAR handover of Skye, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Skye now, here in general practice.
Before Skye goes home, what would you tell him and what follow-up would you arrange?
expect:
• Identify: self, final-year medical student. Skye, 33, mechanic.
  • Situation: 5 months of fatigue with polyuria, nocturia and thirst. New type 2 diabetes. Well, no ketones.
  • Background: hypertension and high cholesterol, on perindopril and atorvastatin. Gained 20 kg. Smokes a pack a week, drinks 1 or 2 wines nightly, takeaway and soft drinks. Mother had type 2 diabetes and died of a heart attack at 66.
  • Assessment: BMI 35, waist 118 cm, BP 142/88, acanthosis, capillary glucose 14.6. Dipstick: glucose 3+, ketones negative, SG 1.020. HbA1c 9.1% (76) and fasting glucose 12.4: diabetes; symptomatic, so no repeat needed. FBC, iron, TSH, calcium, EUC normal: no other cause found on bloods; possible coexisting OSA to assess. ALT 64/GGT 92: likely fatty liver ± alcohol. TG 3.4, HDL 0.8: insulin-resistance pattern; LDL 3.0 on atorvastatin. uACR 0.6, eGFR >90: normal baseline, metformin safe.
  • Recommendation: start metformin and lifestyle change, a chronic condition management plan, educator and dietitian, retinal exam. Review in 2 to 4 weeks. Please review the plan.

Most likely: new type 2 diabetes with obesity and metabolic syndrome. Supporting features: thirst, polyuria and nocturia, 20 kg weight gain, BMI 35 with acanthosis, a mother with type 2 diabetes, a high-sugar diet, hypertension and dyslipidaemia, glycosuria, HbA1c 9.1% and fasting glucose 12.4.

  • Diabetes insipidus: fits the polyuria, but he has had no lithium or head injury, the urine is not dilute and contains glucose, and his hyperglycaemia fully explains the polyuria.
  • Hypothyroidism: fits the fatigue and weight gain, but there are no other features and TSH is normal.
  • Depression: fits the fatigue, but he has no low mood or anhedonia.
  • Obstructive sleep apnoea (coexisting): snoring, unrefreshing sleep, BMI 35, neck 43 cm, hypertension and nocturia fit; no witnessed apnoeas or drowsy driving.
  • Type 1 diabetes or LADA (must not miss): he is young, but he is obese with no weight loss and no ketones.

1. Explain the diagnosis in plain words and check understanding.
  2. Lifestyle: quit smoking (Quitline, NRT or varenicline). No more than 10 standard drinks a week and no more than 4 on any day. At least 150 minutes of moderate activity a week. Water instead of soft drinks, less takeaway, aim to lose 5 to 10% of body weight.
  3. Metformin first line: low dose with meals, increased slowly; warn about gut side effects. Credit: target HbA1c generally 7.0% (53) or less; if above target at 3 months, add an SGLT2 inhibitor, GLP-1 RA, DPP-4 inhibitor or sulfonylurea; insulin later if needed.
  4. Team: GP chronic condition management plan, diabetes educator, dietitian, exercise physiologist. NDSS registration.
  5. Complications and risk: retinal exam now, feet, yearly uACR and eGFR. BP above target: aim below 130/80 for people with diabetes, if tolerated (Australian guideline for assessing and managing cardiovascular disease risk 2023; RACGP handbook). Both readings (142/88 and 140/86) are above this. Confirm with home or ambulatory readings, then up-titrate perindopril. Review statin adherence and dose.
  6. Credit: yearly influenza and pneumococcal vaccination; home glucose testing is not routinely needed on metformin alone.

• Go to ED or call 000: vomiting, abdominal pain, fast or deep breathing, drowsiness or confusion, or unable to keep fluids down. Stop metformin while vomiting or dehydrated; also withhold perindopril while vomiting or dehydrated (sick-day rules). If an SGLT2 inhibitor is started, withhold it during acute illness, poor intake or before surgery (euglycaemic ketoacidosis).
  • See the GP sooner: worsening thirst or urination, weight loss, blurred vision, infections, or metformin side effects he cannot tolerate.
  • His questions: insulin is not needed now and may never be. He does not have to stop drinking completely, but should stay within the limits. No sleeping tablet: the night-time urination should settle as his glucose comes down; review sleep and snoring at follow-up.
  • Follow-up: review in 2 to 4 weeks (metformin tolerance, BP, referrals). HbA1c in 3 months. Yearly cycle of care. Written information from Diabetes Australia and the NDSS.

ddx.dx: Type 2 diabetes (new diagnosis) with obesity and metabolic syndrome
ddx.for: Thirst over 3 L a day, nocturia, 20 kg weight gain, BMI 35 with acanthosis, a mother with type 2 diabetes, glycosuria, and HbA1c 9.1% with fasting glucose 12.4.
Fatigue with large-volume polyuria, nocturia and thirst.
ddx.against: No lithium or head injury, his urine is not dilute (SG 1.020) and is full of glucose, and his hyperglycaemia fully explains the polyuria.
No cold intolerance, constipation or skin change, no goitre, normal reflexes, and TSH 1.7.

ddx.for: Fatigue, needing more sleep, and he has stopped exercising.
ddx.against: No low mood, anhedonia or suicidal thoughts, and his thirst and polyuria are explained by hyperglycaemia.

ddx.for: Unrefreshing sleep, snoring, BMI 35, central obesity, hypertension, nocturia.
ddx.against: No witnessed apnoeas, no sleepiness at the wheel; osmotic symptoms explained by hyperglycaemia.

ddx.dx: Type 1 diabetes or latent autoimmune diabetes in adults, with a risk of ketoacidosis
ddx.for: Age 33 with marked hyperglycaemia and osmotic symptoms.
ddx.against: He is obese with weight gain, acanthosis, hypertension and dyslipidaemia, has no weight loss, and urine ketones are negative.

guide:
In Part 1, give findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they would examine. Skye mentions his nocturia only when asked about sleep, the toilet or drinking, and then he asks why it happens. If the candidate asks for a urine dipstick, say the result will come in Part 2; do not mark its interpretation in Part 1. Item 8 rewards a broad screen of systems: tick each cluster asked about. Five or more of seven clusters = full marks; 3 to 4 = partial; fewer than 3 = not awarded.

In Part 2, hand over all three results together and ask the four questions in order. Skye stays quiet during the handover. He puts his Part 2 questions while the candidate explains the plan and safety netting. Items 22-24 may be earned in the handover or in the answer on diagnosis.

A high-performing candidate characterises the fatigue, finds the polyuria, polydipsia and weight gain, and screens widely by system, including sleep, mood and suicidal ideation. They quantify smoking and alcohol and examine for acanthosis, complications and other causes. In Part 2 they explain why no repeat test is needed, use the glucose-laden urine that is not dilute to rule out diabetes insipidus, keep coexisting sleep apnoea in mind, and give a structured plan: lifestyle, metformin, the team, screening for complications, cardiovascular risk and specific red flags.

A borderline candidate takes a narrow history and misses the urinary symptoms. They skip the mood screen, or order a repeat test that is not needed. They start insulin without a reason, or give vague safety netting such as "come back if worse".
explain:
Approaching fatigue

Fatigue is a common, non-specific presentation. Cast the net wide, then use the pattern and timeline. Screen by clusters:

  • endocrine: diabetes, hypothyroidism, hypercalcaemia;
  • anaemia and iron deficiency;
  • malignancy, including haematological malignancy;
  • chronic kidney, liver, heart and lung disease, and infection (such as TB);
  • sleep disorders;
  • depression and substance use, including suicidal ideation;
  • medicines.

Malignancy is less likely in a young adult but should still be considered. Skye's key clues are the osmotic symptoms: polyuria, nocturia that does not settle when he drinks less in the evening, and thirst of over 3 L a day. With 20 kg of weight gain, a high-sugar diet, hypertension, dyslipidaemia, smoking and a mother with type 2 diabetes, they point to type 2 diabetes.

Do not put all of his fatigue down to hyperglycaemia. Skye snores, wakes unrefreshed, and has a BMI of 35, a neck circumference of 43 cm and treated hypertension. OSA often coexists with obesity and type 2 diabetes and also causes nocturia; assess with STOP-Bang or the Epworth scale and refer for a sleep study if fatigue or sleepiness persists once glucose is controlled, or sooner if he is sleepy driving.

Diagnosing diabetes (RACGP handbook)

Diabetes is diagnosed by any one of:

  • HbA1c of 6.5% (48 mmol/mol) or more;
  • fasting plasma glucose of 7.0 mmol/L or more;
  • random plasma glucose of 11.1 mmol/L or more;
  • a 2-hour glucose of 11.1 mmol/L or more on an oral glucose tolerance test.

A person without symptoms needs a second abnormal test on another day. A person with typical symptoms needs only one. Skye is symptomatic and has two different abnormal tests on the same sample, so no repeat is needed.

Interpreting the results

  • Urine: glycosuria means plasma glucose is above the renal threshold. Skye's glucose 3+ is heavy glycosuria. The resulting osmotic diuresis causes polyuria, nocturia and thirst. In diabetes insipidus the urine is dilute (SG typically 1.005 or less) and has no glucose, so Skye's urine, which is not dilute (SG 1.020) and has glucose 3+, argues strongly against it. The dipstick SG pad measures ionic concentration, so glucose adds little to it. Negative ketones are reassuring.
  • Type 1 diabetes or LADA: consider these in a younger, leaner person, or with weight loss, ketones or a rapid onset. Skye has none of these.
  • Other bloods: the normal FBC, iron studies, TSH, calcium and renal function remove the other common treatable causes of fatigue.
  • Liver and lipids: the mildly raised ALT and GGT suggest fatty liver (MASLD) and/or alcohol. Check hepatitis B and C serology (iron studies already normal) as part of excluding other causes. Consider liver ultrasound and, as he gets older, fibrosis assessment (FIB-4 is not validated under 35; elastography if concerned). High triglycerides with low HDL is the pattern of insulin resistance.
  • Kidneys: the normal uACR and eGFR are his baseline and allow metformin.

Initial management (RACGP handbook, eTG)

  • Lifestyle comes first and continues throughout:
    • stop smoking;
    • alcohol: no more than 10 standard drinks a week and no more than 4 on any day (NHMRC);
    • at least 150 minutes of moderate activity a week, plus resistance exercise;
    • dietary change with a dietitian, starting with water instead of soft drinks;
    • weight loss: 5 to 10% improves glycaemia, and more can bring remission.
  • Metformin is first-line unless contraindicated. Start low with food and increase gradually (or use the extended-release form) to limit gut side effects. For example (eTG): 500 mg once daily with the evening meal, increased every 1 to 2 weeks to 1 g twice daily as tolerated, or modified-release 500 mg once daily up to 2 g once daily.
  • Target: an individualised HbA1c, generally 7.0% (53 mmol/mol) or less. A tighter target can be considered in younger people early in the disease if it can be reached safely.
  • Add-on therapy: if HbA1c stays above target, add an SGLT2 inhibitor, GLP-1 receptor agonist, DPP-4 inhibitor or sulfonylurea. An SGLT2 inhibitor or GLP-1 receptor agonist is preferred when there is cardiovascular disease, heart failure or CKD, and a GLP-1 receptor agonist helps with weight. Because Skye's HbA1c is more than 1.5% above target, early combination therapy (metformin with an SGLT2 inhibitor or GLP-1 receptor agonist, the latter favoured for weight) is also reasonable, subject to PBS criteria. Insulin is used later if needed, or earlier with marked symptomatic hyperglycaemia, weight loss or ketosis.
  • Team care: a GP chronic condition management plan gives Medicare-subsidised visits to a diabetes educator, dietitian, exercise physiologist and podiatrist. Registering with the NDSS gives subsidised supplies and education.
  • Glucose monitoring: home testing is not routinely needed on metformin alone. It is used with insulin or sulfonylureas, or as the educator advises.

Complications and cardiovascular risk

  • Screen at diagnosis and then through the annual cycle of care: a retinal examination, a foot assessment, uACR and eGFR, BP, lipids and weight.
  • His BP is above target: aim below 130/80 for people with diabetes, if tolerated (Australian guideline for assessing and managing cardiovascular disease risk 2023; RACGP handbook). Both readings (142/88 and 140/86) are above this. Confirm with home or ambulatory readings, then up-titrate perindopril.
  • RACGP handbook lipid target in type 2 diabetes: LDL below 2.0 mmol/L; LDL 3.0 is above this, so confirm daily adherence, then increase the atorvastatin dose (or add ezetimibe).
  • Vaccines: a yearly influenza vaccine, and pneumococcal vaccination as the Australian Immunisation Handbook recommends for people with diabetes.
  • His father's colon cancer diagnosed at 79 places Skye in the near-average risk group for bowel cancer screening (from age 45).

Safety netting

Vomiting, abdominal pain, rapid or deep breathing, drowsiness or being unable to keep fluids down may be a hyperglycaemic emergency and need ED. Metformin should be withheld while vomiting or dehydrated, and so should his perindopril (sick-day rules). If an SGLT2 inhibitor is added, it should be withheld during acute illness, poor intake or before surgery because of the risk of euglycaemic ketoacidosis. Worsening osmotic symptoms or weight loss need earlier GP review. Review him in 2 to 4 weeks for tolerance and BP, check HbA1c at 3 months, and continue the annual cycle of care.
points: Approach fatigue with a broad screen by symptom clusters (endocrine, anaemia, malignancy, organ failure, sleep, mood and substances, medicines), then use the pattern and timeline. Always ask about suicidal ideation.
Polyuria, nocturia that persists despite drinking less in the evening, thirst and weight gain in someone with metabolic risk factors point to type 2 diabetes.
With typical symptoms, one HbA1c of 6.5% (48 mmol/mol) or more, or a fasting glucose of 7.0 mmol/L or more, diagnoses diabetes; without symptoms, repeat the test on another day.
Glucose-laden urine that is not dilute means an osmotic diuresis, not diabetes insipidus. Negative ketones are against ketoacidosis and type 1 diabetes.

Initial management is lifestyle change (smoking, alcohol, activity, diet, weight) with metformin first line, team care under a GP chronic condition management plan, NDSS registration, baseline screening for complications, and BP and lipid management.
Safety net for a hyperglycaemic emergency (vomiting, abdominal pain, rapid breathing, drowsiness) and review in 2 to 4 weeks, with HbA1c at 3 months.
